subtitle: GROWTH CHAMBER · PRE-PIVOT  ·  WEEK
title: Sourcing finished, purchasing frozen
context: Our first plan was a sealed growth chamber with hydroponics inside it. Arabidopsis needs steady humidity, temperature and light to give comparable results, and the school lab could not hold any of those steady. The chamber was meant to give us a controlled box to run every plant experiment in. This was the last week of design before we started buying parts.

body.v: Finished the chamber layout and ran airflow studies on the enclosure.
Fans, ducting and shelf spacing sized around a   how many trays?   tray capacity.
Built four sourcing lists, split by where we would actually buy each part.
Electronics and control from Guanghua. Structure from Test Rite. Plants and water systems from the Jianguo flower market. Containers from IKEA.
Fans, timers, DS18B20 temperature sensors, blackout cloth, a Mylar substitute, air pumps and air stones.
Total came to   NT$ ?  .
Stopped on 28 March, told to buy nothing and print nothing.
The instructors were still weighing the effort against the risk and against what the chamber would be worth to us later.
Nothing had been ordered, so the freeze cost us planning time and nothing else.

decision: Freeze purchasing instead of building in parallel
If half of it was already built we’d have argued to keep going.
We hadn’t spent anything yet, so stopping was free.
counter: Ordering the slow-delivery parts anyway to keep the option open. Nobody had defended the chamber yet, so that would have been buying our way into a decision.

problems.what: We picked the chamber before checking it was the right build
problems.fix: Wait for the instructors’ evaluation before any further design work, and agree a hardware budget before the next sourcing round.

next: Read the new direction document when it lands. Brainstorm against it before defending the chamber.

subtitle: HUMIDITY BOX · ORIGIN  ·  WEEK
title: Visiting Prof. Verslues
context: We had a chamber design nobody had agreed to and a purchasing freeze. None of us had seen a working plant growth setup, so we went to look at one before designing any more of our own.

body.v: Visited Prof. Verslues at   institution   on 3 April.
He works on   his research area  .
Looked at how his incubator holds conditions across a whole tray at once.
Trays sit on wire shelving with airflow coming from underneath.
He grows at a much lower density than we had been planning for.
Came back and dropped the full chamber in favour of a humidity box.
Humidity is the condition that decides whether the seeds come up, and a box holding one tray is a build we could actually finish.

decision: Build a humidity box, not a growth chamber
Small enough that we’d actually finish it.
Humidity is the condition that decides whether the seeds come up.
counter: Carrying on with the full chamber. It was frozen anyway, and after seeing a real one we couldn’t justify the size.

problems.what: No target humidity range written down, and nothing to measure it with
problems.fix: Get the range Arabidopsis needs, and put a sensor on the next electronics order.

next: Design the box around a target humidity range, not around the space we happen to have.

subtitle: DIRECTION · PROF. CHEN  ·  CONSULTATION
title: Told to drop soil sensing
context: Our original plan was to sense drought stress in soil and release protectant into the soil directly. Before committing to it we wanted someone who sells into agriculture to tell us whether it held up.

body.v: Had an online meeting with Prof. Chen of   institution  , who works on   field  , on 10 April.
He has commercial products in the smart agriculture market we were aiming at.
Were told to drop soil moisture sensing entirely.
Cheap sensors already dominate that market and they are inaccurate.
Calibrating a sensor across soil types takes three to four months of data for each one.
Took his second point, that soil release is hard to defend on biosafety.
Engineered bacteria going into open soil is a much harder case to make than bacteria kept inside a vessel. He pushed us toward containment.
Reframed the business model around the consumable rather than the device.
Sell the cartridge, not the box, the way printers and ink work. His idea, not ours.
Drop soil sensing and move to a contained vessel
A market already served by cheap sensors is not one we can enter with a school budget.
Containment is easier to defend than release, and we were going to be asked about it.

counter: Soil calibration across types. Three to four months of data for each one, which we do not have.
[[ anything else from the meeting ]]

problems.what: No bioreactor design exists yet
problems.fix: Ask Dr. Pak for the reactor landscape before choosing a configuration.

problems.what: Soil compatibility now unclaimable
problems.fix: If we ever claim it, it needs the 3–4 months of data per soil he described.

next: Get the reactor families from Dr. Pak so the new direction has a shape.

subtitle: BIOREACTOR · CONCEPT  ·  CONSULTATION
title: The pivot, and asking Dr. Pak where to start
context: This is the week the project changed shape. The pivot document went up on 15 April: instead of sensing soil and releasing into it, engineered B. subtilis would live inside a sealed vessel, and light would tell them when to produce protectant. That vessel is a bioreactor, and none of us had built one or knew where to start.

body.v: Posted the pivot on 15 April. Input soil stress, output green or red light into a contained chamber.
Seven people reacted to the message. Every instrument in this notebook follows from it.
Asked Dr. Pak, Dean of Research, for the reactor landscape.
He set out five families. Continuous stirred tank, bubble column, air lift, fluidised bed, packed bed.
He suggested a packed bed for our case, with bacteria immobilised in the column.
He said bioreactor design is an enormous field and there is no need to invent something new. Adapting a common design to our needs would itself be the achievement.
We went on to choose hollow-fibre tangential flow, which is not what he suggested. That conversation happened in person and nobody wrote down why.
what else happened this week?

decision: Adapt an existing reactor design rather than invent one
Adapting an existing design became the goal, so the scope stopped growing.
Five families to choose from instead of a blank page.
counter: Nothing yet. Hollow fibre was recommended in person and nobody wrote it down, so we can’t say why we didn’t take the packed-bed suggestion.
[[ photo from this week ]]
[[ photo from this week ]]

problems.what: No record of why hollow fibre over packed bed
problems.fix: Ask Dr. Pak to put the reasoning in a message so it exists in writing.

problems.what: No selection criteria were written down
problems.fix: Write the criteria out now and mark them as reconstructed.

next: Specify a hollow-fibre configuration we can actually buy in Taipei.

subtitle: HYDROPONICS · ASSAY STANDARD  ·  WEEK
title: Working out what a stress assay should measure
context: The pivot had landed but the plant side of the project had no experiment behind it. Before building anything for the plants we needed to agree what stress we would apply, at what level, and what we would measure to say whether the protectant worked.

body.v: Argued out what a standard stress assay would look like for us.
Salinity came up more than heat, mostly because it is easier to apply consistently.
what did you settle on, and what was still open?
anything built or ordered this week?

problems.what: No agreed stress assay
problems.fix: Pick the stress, the concentration and the readout, and write them down.

subtitle: LOW ACTIVITY WEEK  ·  WEEK
title: Nothing much happened

body.v: what was happening this week? exams, holidays, other coursework?
anything ticking over in the background?

problems.what: A week lost with nothing scheduled
problems.fix: Agree deadlines per task so gaps are planned instead of discovered.

subtitle: MILESTONES  ·  WEEK
title: Four instruments, three people
context: The instructors asked for a milestone and a deadline against every task in the project. Writing the list turned out to be more useful than the list itself.

body.v: Listed every task in progress with an owner and a date.
Two tasks had no owner at all until the list was written.
Found we had four instruments in progress and three people to lead them.
Humidity box, imaging station, light plate, fluorometer, with the bioreactor about to start.
Left the fluorometer decision to the following week.
Nothing was built this week. The output was an uncomfortable conclusion.

problems.what: Four instruments, not enough people
problems.fix: Drop one. Decide which next week.

subtitle: FLUOROMETER · PHOTOMETER  ·  WEEK
title: Dropping the fluorometer
context: The chlorophyll fluorometer would have let us measure plant stress directly, by reading damage to photosystem II. Fv/Fm is the standard number for that, and a healthy plant sits around 0.78 to 0.83. It was the fourth instrument we had in progress and there were three of us.

body.v: Made the case for building it.
It measures the outcome the project claims to improve, so it would test our own claim directly.
Commercial meters run past NT$100,000 and the open-source Open-JIP design already exists, so the gap looked worth closing.
Dropped it on 11 May, on capacity rather than feasibility.
Anton moved to the bioreactor. Eva took a different task.
The Open-JIP evaluation was never written up, so anyone picking it up starts from nothing.
Wrote the photometer requirement on 16 May, in nine words.
We need to measure flow rate, and how much B. subtilis there is.
The shape of the answer followed immediately: flow cuvette plus spectrometer, 600 nm beam, a sensor reading light decay, an intensity controller.
Drop the fluorometer on capacity, not feasibility
The science holds up. It was never a feasibility problem, only a staffing one.
Better to finish two instruments than half-finish three.

counter: Building it anyway with a part-time lead. Three half-finished instruments is worse than two finished and one we admit we skipped.
[[ photometer sketch or spec ]]
[[ bench this week ]]

problems.what: No direct measure of plant stress response
problems.fix: Either source a commercial meter for final validation, or state the gap on the wiki.

problems.what: Open-JIP evaluation never written up
problems.fix: Write it up anyway so a future team can start from it.

next: Specify the photometer optics. Flow cuvette, beam path, and what the sensor actually reads.

subtitle: HUMIDITY BOX · IMAGING STATION  ·  BUILD
title: Humidity box finished, agar photos useless
context: The humidity box is a small sealed enclosure that keeps humidity steady while Arabidopsis germinates. It came out of the Verslues visit and it is the first thing we finished. The same week we started growing on agar plates, and ran into a problem we had not planned for.

body.v: Finished the humidity box and put the first seeds in.
It holds   target humidity and temperature  , though we have no log of what it actually holds.
Started photographing agar plates to track germination. The photos were useless.
The angle moved between shots, the room light changed with the time of day, and the shadows moved with it.
Two plates photographed on different days told us nothing about how much had grown.
Spent two afternoons shooting a transparent dish on a white table, trying to find a repeatable setup by hand.
It did not work, but it told us what was moving: angle, distance, background and ambient light.
A fix has to hold all four at once, which a person with a phone cannot do.
Both of us kept working on the other one.

decision: Build a station instead of writing a procedure
A written procedure still depends on whoever is holding the phone.
If the geometry is locked in plastic, the photos come out comparable whether you’re careful or not.
counter: A tripod and a taped mark on the bench. Cheaper, does nothing about room light, and it’s wrong the moment someone moves the tripod.
angle trial
lighting trial

problems.what: Humidity box has no recorded target range
problems.fix: Log the humidity and temperature it actually holds, and over what period.

problems.what: No way yet to compare plates across days
problems.fix: Build the station. Lock the phone, the light and the background.

next: Design and build the imaging station around the four variables the hand tests exposed.

subtitle: IMAGING STATION  ·  BUILD
title: Building the agar plate imaging station
context: The imaging station is a rig that holds a phone in a fixed position over an agar plate, under fixed lighting, so photos taken days apart can be compared. It is the answer to the problem from last week.

body.v: Built a four-legged frame with a slot at the top for the phone.
The phone contacts the corner and locks, which fixes position and angle with no moving parts.
Added a dark lid so no room light reaches the plate, and an LED ring inside as the only light source.

We wanted the light in a circle and angled in toward the plate. Bending an LED strip into an angled circle makes it twist and compress along its length at once, and it buckles somewhere unpredictable.
Putting ridges around the ring fixed it. The strip creases at each ridge, the tension goes out, and the creases land where we chose.
Cut a slot with two guide rails so the strip slides in instead of being glued down.
A dead LED can be replaced without reprinting the ring, which takes six hours.
Made the white bottom plate removable from underneath on four screws.
Swap it for black and the photo background changes with no reprint. Every part of the station comes apart the same way.

photos: LED strip seated in the slot
decision: Ridges to take the tension out, and a slide-in slot
Creasing at the ridges is predictable. Left alone the strip buckles wherever it wants.
With a slot we can replace the strip without reprinting the ring.
counter: Gluing the strip onto a smooth angled ring. It works against the strip, and replacing an LED would mean reprinting the part.

problems.what: Lighting evenness across the plate never measured
problems.fix: Photograph a blank plate and check for a brightness gradient across the frame.

problems.what: No fixed camera settings recorded
problems.fix: Lock exposure and white balance, and write the settings into the protocol.

next: Use it on the real salinity plates and find out whether day-to-day comparison holds up.

subtitle: LIGHT PLATE · LPA-1  ·  BUILD
title: Assembly guide tested by handing it over
context: The light plate, later called DiOPAL, shines green and red light into wells of bacteria. Green switches the CcaS-CcaR circuit on and red switches it off, so the plate is how we control when the bacteria produce. Prototype 1 only had to prove we could light 24 wells evenly.

body.v: Seated the 24-well printed plate and wired the Arduino and breadboard to the first row.
Nothing is soldered. It is all breadboard and jumper leads.
Wrote the assembly guide to step level, each step small enough to stop between.
LPA_Assembly_Guide_v2.docx,   how many steps?   steps.
Stopped at step 15 on purpose and left a note to continue from step 16.
The next person picked it up from the document alone with no verbal handoff. It is the only check we have that the guide is good enough for someone else to build from.
It needs filing on the long axis and the school closed on us. Cosmetic for prototype 1, and the lid geometry changes at prototype 2 anyway.
Parts as actually fitted. The lid fault is recorded here rather than left to the photographs.

photos: LED harness in the first row
decision: Leave the lid and write it down
It does not block the 13 June date, and that is the only date that matters this month.
The geometry changes at prototype 2, so any fix now gets thrown away.
counter: Reprinting at a looser tolerance. Nine hours of print time against five minutes with a file.
guide open at step 15
plate handed over mid-build

problems.what: SINCE W12
problems.fix: Lux meter at each of the 24 wells at fixed height, one pass per channel.

problems.what: Lid does not seat
problems.fix: File the long axis, then measure what came off so prototype 2 starts there.

problems.what: Nothing soldered yet, it is all breadboard
problems.fix: Solder the harness once the well spacing is final.

next: Measure homogeneity. It is the stated acceptance criterion and we have not checked it once.

subtitle: BIOREACTOR · PROTOTYPE I  ·  BUILD
title: Bioreactor prototype I built
context: The bioreactor is the vessel the pivot committed us to. Bacteria live inside a hollow fibre membrane while the protectant they make crosses the membrane and leaves, which keeps the organism contained. Prototype I is the simplest version of that we could build.

body.v: Built prototype I on 6 June from four parts.
PES hollow fibre membrane with around 200 mL of lumen volume, a 500 mL reservoir holding 300 mL of LB, a peristaltic pump, and a luer valve on the loop for sampling.
Inoculated with 20 mL of a multi-overnight B. subtilis culture.
Deliberately left everything else off. No stirring, no aeration, no pH control.
We did not know which of those we needed. Starting with none means every addition later has a reason behind it we can point at.
Adding them all at once would have meant several things failing together with no way to tell which mattered.
Drove both light plate wavelengths for the first time, green 520 nm and red 660 nm.
First row of wells only, driven independently. Green is the on command for the CcaS-CcaR circuit and red is the off command.
Built the round vertical agar stand.
what is it for, and how does it differ from the square one?
TABLE 9
Prototype I as built on 6 June. Simple continuous flow-through, nothing active in the reservoir.

photos: light plate, first light in both colours
decision: Build the simplest loop we can
Each thing we add later then has a reason behind it we can point at.
It also means the first run tells us something even if it fails.
counter: Building it fully specified from the start. More parts failing together, and no way to attribute anything.

problems.what: No active mixing, and the sampling port is on the loop rather than the reservoir
problems.fix: Add a stirrer if growth is poor, and move the port to the reservoir outlet where there is more volume.

problems.what: No temperature control on the loop
problems.fix: Decide whether we run at room temperature or in the incubator, and keep it the same between runs.

next: Run it and get a growth curve against a flask control.

subtitle: BIOREACTOR · PROTOTYPE I  ·  FAILURE DIAGNOSIS
title: The cells barely grow in the reactor
context: This is the first run of prototype I. We grew the same culture in the reactor and in a flask at the same time, both at room temperature, so the flask acts as a control. If the reactor works, the two curves should look alike.

body.v: Sampled both arms every thirty minutes for eight hours, then again at 25 hours.
One person had to stay with it for the whole run.
Got a flask that climbed past 2.4 and a reactor that stayed almost flat near 0.3.
The numbers inside the system disagreed too, 0.304 in the tube against 0.48 in the reservoir. That should not happen if the loop is mixed.
Terminated early when medium leaked at the peristaltic pump.
The leak was at the pump head, where the tubing flexes most.
That is our evidence the membrane holds the bacteria in. It came out of the run that otherwise failed.
Ruled out means we ran the test. To test means we have not.

photos: Paired growth curves against a flask control at room temperature. The flask climbed past 2.4 over 25 hours. The reactor stayed almost flat and ended near 0.3, and the run terminated early on a leak at the pump.
reactor and flask side by side
decision: Change three things at once and accept we will not know which worked
Stirring, temperature and sampling position are all cheap to change and all plausible.
We have weeks, not months. We couldn’t afford to change one thing at a time.
counter: Testing one variable at a time. That’s the right way to do it and we chose speed instead. Writing it down here so nobody reads prototype II as proof that stirring alone fixed it.
shell-side plate, no colonies
pump head where it leaked

problems.what: Three variables change together in prototype II
problems.fix: Any of the three could be the real cause. Say that, instead of claiming stirring fixed it.

problems.what: Leak at the peristaltic pump
problems.fix: Upgrade to BPT tubing before the next run.

next: Prototype II. Magnetic stirring at 200 rpm, sampling moved to the reservoir outlet, run at 37 °C.

subtitle: BIOREACTOR · PROTOTYPE II  ·  TEST
title: Prototype II reaches plateau in two hours
context: Prototype I barely grew and we had four candidate reasons. Prototype II changes three of them at once, which is not how you isolate a cause, but we had weeks rather than months.

body.v: Added a 200 rpm magnetic stirrer to the reservoir to stop cells settling out.
The stirrer bar was the largest one we had, which may be part of why it worked so well.
Moved the sampling port to the reservoir outlet, where there is far more volume.
A sample from there represents the whole system rather than one length of tube.
Ran both arms at 37 °C instead of room temperature, pump held at 94 mL/min.
Got a full growth curve, and the reactor beat its own flask control.
Reactor plateaued at OD600 0.8 to 0.9 after two hours. Flask reached 0.6 to 0.8 after four and a half.
TABLE 11
Full growth curve secured. The reactor reached plateau faster and higher than the flask.

decision: Passed. Faster to plateau and higher than the control
Faster to plateau and higher at plateau than the control, which is more than we expected.
Whether stirring alone would have done it, we cannot say.
counter: Claiming stirring fixed it. Three variables moved and only one of them is in the headline.

problems.what: Three changes at once, so we cannot say which one did it
problems.fix: Run stirring alone at 22 °C, which also gets us the temperature we would actually operate at.

next: Evaluate at 22 °C, and upgrade to BPT tubing to stop the degradation seen in earlier trials.

subtitle: BIOREACTOR · PROF. CHANG  ·  CONSULTATION
title: Prof. Chang finds the gap in the design
context: Prof. Chang is a chair professor in chemical engineering at NCKU who has published on B. subtilis bioreactor systems, so he was the right person to show the design to. He found a hole in it that none of us had seen.

body.v: Showed him the design in person on 18 June.
He spent longer on containment than on the biology, which we had not expected.
Were told the hollow fibre and the light module are the parts that make the project distinctive.
But we need to be able to explain to a judge why hollow fibre specifically, and we could not.
Took the main criticism. We had no mechanism at all for getting protectant out of the membrane.
His suggestion was a valve after the membrane, to build pressure and push the permeate through.
Posted a stepper pinch valve design to the build channel the next day, with a 27 June target.
There was no valve on any plan before we spoke to him.
Foaming from B. subtilis surfactant, which he mentioned twice. Resting cells. The cartridge format.

photos: hollow fibre module, the part he questioned
decision: Add a valve after the membrane
A valve after the membrane is the mechanism we were missing entirely.
Hydroponics as the delivery target, which also narrows the biosafety case.
Membrane sizing becomes a design variable rather than a fixed part.
counter: Resting cells, and the cartridge format. Raised in the meeting, no design response yet.

problems.what: Foaming not addressed
problems.fix: Raised twice, no response. Add a foam trap or say why we didn’t.

problems.what: Lux to PPFD conversion never recorded
problems.fix: Write down the factor we used and where it came from. Every light dose we quote rests on it.

next: Post the pinch valve design and set a print date. Chang’s other points still need answers.

subtitle: LIGHT PLATE · DOSE UNITS  ·  TEST
title: Wrong unit for the light dose
context: The CcaS-CcaR circuit responds to a specific photon flux, so the light dose the plate delivers has to be a known quantity. This week we found we had been about to measure it in entirely the wrong unit.

body.v: Checked the Castillo-Hair paper and found its half-maximal point is 4.66 µmol per square metre per second.
That is a photon flux density. It counts photons.
Checked what our meters read, and found every affordable one reads illuminance in lux.
Lux is weighted for human vision, which peaks around 555 nm. Our green sits at 520 and our red at 660, both well off that peak.
So the conversion error is not even the same size on the two channels.
Bought a lux meter and set out to derive the conversion for our own LED spectra.
A proper PPFD sensor was out of budget. A phone app was considered and rejected as not repeatable between handsets.
Caught it before any dose figure went out, so nothing published needs correcting.
The factor we actually used is   what factor did you use, and where from?   and is not written down anywhere.
Table 12a. The two units measure different things and cannot be converted without knowing the spectrum.

decision: Buy a lux meter and derive the conversion ourselves
A proper PPFD sensor was out of budget and we needed a number that week.
counter: Quoting the paper’s number in lux and hoping. Every dose we published afterwards would have been wrong by a factor nobody could reproduce.
LED spectra, green and red
meter reading at a well

problems.what: The conversion factor we used is not written down anywhere
problems.fix: Find it, write it down with the spectrum assumption, and restate every dose figure in PPFD.

problems.what: Green and red need different factors
problems.fix: Compute both from the LED spectra rather than using one number for the plate.

next: Write the factor down. Until it exists, no light dose in this project is reproducible.

subtitle: STRESS TO LIGHT · FIRMWARE  ·  BUILD
title: Temperature sensor driving the green channel
context: The whole project is one sentence: sense stress, emit light, release protectant. This is the first time the sensing end and the light end ran together on a bench, two months after the pivot.

body.v: Wired an SHT31 temperature and humidity sensor to the Arduino over I2C.
It reports humidity too, which the code reads and then ignores.
Wrote a linear stress fraction between a floor and a ceiling temperature.
Below 32 °C the LED is off. At 50 °C and above it is at full brightness. Between those it scales linearly.
Mapped the fraction onto a PWM green channel and ran it.
The transfer function is four lines of code, deliberately. Anything more shaped would be invented, since we have no data on how stress response scales with temperature.
Wrote it up as Stress_to_Light_Demo_Manual.docx.
32 °C and 50 °C are guesses, not measurements. Only the green channel is driven, so the demo switches the circuit on but not off.
Table 12b. Four constants and a straight line between two of them.

decision: Linear between two thresholds, nothing more shaped
Two thresholds are easy to change once the wet lab gives us real numbers.
Anything more shaped would be a guess dressed up as a model.
counter: A sigmoid or a lookup table. Neither is supported by anything we measured.
serial output, stress fraction
LED at full duty

problems.what: TEMP_BASE and TEMP_MAX are guesses
problems.fix: Get the real heat-stress thresholds for Arabidopsis from the wet lab and replace them.

problems.what: Red channel not in the loop
problems.fix: Add the OFF command so the demo shows both directions, not just on.

problems.what: Humidity is read but not used
problems.fix: The SHT31 gives it for free. Decide whether it should feed the stress fraction.

next: Replace the placeholder thresholds with numbers from the wet lab.

subtitle: HYDROPONICS · FLOATING PLATE  ·  BUILD
title: Making the plate float
context: Arabidopsis grows hydroponically on a plate sitting over liquid medium. The roots have to reach the liquid without the plate flooding, and our first version was fixed in place, which meant setting the level by hand every day and getting it wrong.

body.v: Built a fixed plate with a liquid chamber underneath, and found the level impossible to hold.
It has to sit as high as possible without coming over the growing platform, and it drops as the plants drink, so the roots end up in air.
Redesigned it to float on the medium instead.
The frame of the platform is built as sealed air chambers, so it rides on the surface and stays at the same height above the liquid whatever the level does.
Calculated the buoyancy before printing rather than tuning it afterwards.
A hollow frame cannot be adjusted once printed, so print orientation and wall thickness now decide whether it floats.
Added poles at the corners to take washers as weights.
Adding weight is easier than adding volume, so the poles are the margin for error. The washers we have are heavier than the calculation wanted, so the adjustment is coarse.
corner poles and washers
floating in medium
Printed the first iteration on 25 June.
later iterations shrank it and added clip-in handles. when?

decision: Float the platform instead of controlling the level
The height stays correct as the medium level drops.
counter: A level sensor and a top-up pump. More parts, more to break, and it solves something the shape solves for nothing.
floating in medium, loaded
freeboard measured

problems.what: Buoyancy not verified with plants on it, and the weight poles may be unnecessary
problems.fix: Float it fully loaded, measure the freeboard, and see whether the washers are needed at all.

next: Print it, float it, and find out how far off the maths was.

subtitle: PHOTOMETER · ITERATION 1  ·  BUILD
title: Iteration 1. Bubbles and drift
context: The photometer measures how much B. subtilis is in the reactor loop without taking samples out. An amber LED shines through a thin flow cuvette and we read how much light gets through. A beamsplitter sends part of the beam to a reference sensor first, so drift in the LED shows up in both channels and divides out.

body.v: Printed a rail where the LED, lens, beamsplitter, cuvette holder and both sensors each position independently.
None of us knew where the components should sit, so we made all of them movable and worked it out on the bench.
Ran the beam horizontally through the flow cuvette and plumbed it into the loop.
Got data that fluctuated far too much to use, for two reasons that made each other worse.
Bubbles formed inside the cuvette and sat in the beam. A bubble moves the reading in a step rather than adding noise around it.
The lens and beamsplitter mounts were loose enough that the alignment drifted while we watched it.
Decided to move the cuvette down to the base for the next build.
Bubbles rise, so putting the cuvette at the bottom takes them out of the beam without us doing anything. A dual luer valve and syringes let us pull gas out on demand.

decision: Move the cuvette to the base
Bubbles rise, so putting the cuvette at the bottom takes them out of the beam without us doing anything.
A dual luer valve and syringes let us pull the gas out on demand.
Mounting vertically at the same time, since the geometry has to change anyway.
counter: A fixed rail with no adjustment. More stable, but no way to find the alignment.

problems.what: Bubbles in the flow cuvette
problems.fix: Move the cuvette to the base and add a dual luer valve and syringes to bleed the gas.

problems.what: Loose lens and beamsplitter tolerances
problems.fix: Tighten the mounts on the next iteration.

next: Rebuild with the cuvette low, tighter tolerances and a way to get the bubbles out.

subtitle: PHOTOMETER · ITERATION 2  ·  TEST
title: Iteration 2. Zeroed against the wrong thing
context: Iteration 1 drifted and bubbled. Iteration 2 moves the cuvette to the base, turns the whole assembly upright and tightens every mount. This is the first time we tested against a sample where we already knew the answer.

body.v: Rebuilt with the cuvette at the base, mounted vertically, tolerances tightened.
Blanked, then read medium alone, then medium with 2 mL of titanium dioxide as a known turbid sample.
The titanium dioxide settles within a couple of minutes, so readings have to be taken promptly after mixing.
Got 62.5 au against a true value of 0.75.
The reference channel held steady at 92.5 lux across both readings, so that part of the design is behaving.
We had zeroed against the medium instead of clear water, so the zero was wrong from the start. Blanking on medium sets zero at a point that already absorbs light.
Every reading after a bad blank carries that error, however good the hardware is.
TABLE 15
True value for the TiO₂ sample is 0.75 au. We were out by roughly 20 %.

photos: blank and sample side by side
decision: Did not pass. The procedure was wrong, not the optics
We zeroed against the medium instead of clear water, so the zero was wrong from the start.
Everything after a bad blank carries that error, no matter how good the optics are.
counter: One reading against one known sample. It tells us the zero was wrong. It doesn’t tell us the instrument is linear.
blank and sample side by side
serial monitor reading

problems.what: Blank taken on medium instead of clear water
problems.fix: Reblank on distilled water and run the same TiO₂ readings again.

problems.what: Component tolerances still loose
problems.fix: Decrease tolerances on the next build.

next: Fix the procedure. Blank on clear water, tighten the tolerances, and run a dilution series.

subtitle: BIOREACTOR · SPEC FREEZE  ·  DECISION
title: Rewriting the spec, and pulling a claim
context: Bioreactor parts had been discussed across four Discord channels and several documents, and the numbers had drifted apart from each other. This week we wrote one specification and checked every line of it against the parts we had actually bought.

body.v: Wrote a single spec and marked what each line supersedes.
Part numbers came off the invoices rather than off the parts, so they should still be checked against what is fitted.
Corrected the microcontroller and the membrane to what we own.
ESP32 with a 12-bit ADC became Arduino Uno R4 with 14-bit. The membrane record became 0.2 µm, 150 cm², eight fibres.
Withdrew our own biosafety claim.
The old spec claimed a 50 kDa molecular weight cut-off and said the membrane blocks outer membrane vesicles. Neither is true of the part we bought.
A 0.2 µm pore passes ACCD at around 36 kDa, which is what we want, but it also passes small vesicles and cell debris.
Kept the one containment claim that still stands.
The membrane does block whole B. subtilis. The shell-side plate in prototype I showed that.
Table 15a. Rows 3 and 4 withdraw a claim we had made.

photos: TFF module label and part number
decision: Retract the containment claim rather than restate it quietly
The pore we bought passes small vesicles and debris, so the old wording claimed more containment than we have.
counter: Leaving the old numbers in, once we had checked them against the datasheet.
membrane datasheet, pore size
Uno R4 fitted

problems.what: Containment now rests on cell size alone
problems.fix: Say exactly what the membrane does and does not stop, on the wiki, in those words.

next: Decide whether a second containment stage is needed now that the first claim is narrower.

subtitle: PHOTOMETER · ITERATION 3  ·  TEST
title: Iteration 3. Response does not double
context: Iteration 2 was zeroed against the wrong reference, so its numbers meant nothing. Iteration 3 fixes the procedure, tilts the stand so bubbles clear, and this time reads two concentrations instead of one so we can see whether the response scales.

body.v: Built iteration 3 with tighter tolerances and a tilted stand.
Blanked on clear water this time rather than on medium.
That gives a zero we can defend.
Read medium, then 1 mL of titanium dioxide, then 2 mL.
Medium reads zero. 1 mL gives 0.3712 au. 2 mL gives 0.5785.
Doubling the concentration gave 1.56 times the OD, not twice it. Either that is real Beer-Lambert behaviour at this path length or our transform is wrong, and two points cannot tell us which.
Noticed two things we cannot explain.
Absolute light dropped hard between builds, 660 lux down to 137. Something changed in the LED drive or the optics and we did not write down which.
The reference moved from 17.23 to 18.33 between readings minutes apart. A reference should not do that.
Two concentrations rather than one. Doubling the TiO₂ moved OD from 0.3712 to 0.5785, not to 0.7424.

decision: Procedure fixed, but the response does not scale
Blanking on water gives us a zero we can defend.
counter: Absolute lux dropped hard between iterations, 660 to 137. Something changed in the LED drive or the optics and we didn’t write down which.
1 mL and 2 mL TiO2
serial reading

problems.what: Response is not proportional to concentration
problems.fix: Run a five-point dilution series from 0.05 to 1.0 OD and plot it.

problems.what: Reference channel drifted between two readings minutes apart
problems.fix: Log the reference on its own for an hour with nothing else changing.

next: Build iteration 4 with the positions locked, then put it on the reactor.

subtitle: BIOREACTOR · PRESSURE  ·  BUILD
title: Transmembrane pressure on a screen
context: A hollow fibre membrane fouls as it runs, and fouling shows up as pressure building across the membrane. Until this week we had no way of seeing that happen, so we could not tell a clean run from a blocked one.

body.v: Fitted a BP8G-AGA pressure transducer on the retentate side.
It reads 0 to 1 MPa and outputs 0 to 5 V. The board input is 0 to 3.3 V, so the divider is not optional.
The divider is on a breadboard rather than soldered, so the reading is only as steady as that joint.
Had transmembrane pressure on a screen by the evening of 12 July.
Logged but never zeroed against atmosphere, so the absolute values are suspect even though the shape is not.
Posted the trace and had the sawtooth on it explained the same day.
Dr. Pak looked at the photograph and asked in one line whether the pulses were the peristaltic pump. They were.
The exchange is in the channel, so we can account for the oscillation.
Instrumented before fitting the pinch valve, even though the valve was designed and waiting.
A valve on a loop we cannot measure tells us nothing, and pressure is what the valve controls.

decision: Instrument the loop before fitting the valve
Put a valve on a loop we can’t measure and we won’t see what it does.
Pressure is what the valve is there to control.
counter: Fitting the pinch valve first, which was already designed and waiting. Ordering it that way would have made the valve’s effect invisible.

problems.what: No pinch valve yet, so pressure cannot be controlled
problems.fix: Print the valve and fit it after the membrane.

problems.what: Sawtooth amplitude never quantified
problems.fix: Measure it peak to peak and check against the pump head rate.

next: Fit the valve. Start the long photometer run on the reactor.

subtitle: LIGHT PLATE · DIOPAL V3  ·  BUILD
title: DiOPAL V3 finished
context: Prototype 1 of the light plate lit one row back on 1 June. Milestone 2 asked for tunable intensity in both colours across the whole array. This is the packaged version, V3.

body.v: Packaged the array into a white well block on a black base, four rows by six columns.
Twenty-four wells, which is more than any experiment we currently have planned needs.
Added a printed light-blocking shroud with a front slider.
The array can be opened without unmounting it. The slider rattles slightly when open, which affects nothing.
from above, both colours
on the base, side on
Drove all channels from the Arduino over PWM on separate pins.
The intensity tiers are set by the wiring as well as the code, because we measured every LED and rewired them by brightness. The tiers hold even if the firmware changes.

decision: Sort the LEDs by hand rather than correct in firmware
LEDs that are supposed to be identical varied enough that PWM alone wouldn’t have kept the tiers apart.
Sorting once is permanent. Correcting each LED in firmware would need redoing whenever one is replaced.
counter: Driving them all at the same duty and living with the spread. HIGH, MID and LOW would have overlapped.

problems.what: SINCE W12
problems.fix: Lux meter at every well at fixed height, then run the optogenetic switch on it.

next: Run a real optogenetic experiment on it. So far we’ve only checked the light.

subtitle: LIGHT PLATE · LED CALIBRATION  ·  TEST
title: Measuring every LED before wiring
context: The intensity tiers on the light plate only mean something if the LEDs inside a tier actually match each other. Before wiring V3 we measured every LED we had bought, one at a time.

body.v: Measured all 20 green and all 20 red LEDs at 5 V with a lux meter.
Two of the reds were dead out of the packet and are not in the counts.
Threw the first round of readings away.
Moving the sensor around the structure changed the reading so much that the numbers were not comparable to each other.
Printed a jig to hold the sensor at a fixed position and did the whole thing again.
The jig fixes height but not angle, so there is still some error we have not quantified.
Found more than 25 percent spread across parts sold as identical.
Greens ranged 2.01 to 2.54 kLux. Reds ranged 360 to 438 lux.
After sorting, the low green tier spans 2.33 to 2.34 and the low red spans 0.390 to 0.397.
We measured green in kLux and red in lux, which we should have caught before writing the table.
TABLE 19
Matched sets after sorting. Greens in kLux, reds in lux, which needs fixing.

photos: LEDs tagged by row and column
decision: Passed. Matched sets hold the tiers apart
Spread inside each tier after sorting is much smaller than the spread we started with.
counter: We characterised the LEDs, not the wells. What reaches each well is still unmeasured.
LEDs sorted into tiers
rewired array

problems.what: Green and red are on different scales
problems.fix: Green is in kLux and red is in lux. Pick one and redo the table.

problems.what: Recalibrated match targets left blank in the doc
problems.fix: Fill in the target lux we recalibrated to, for green and for red.

next: Measure light at the wells, not at the LEDs. That’s the acceptance criterion still open from May.

subtitle: PHOTOMETER · ON THE REACTOR  ·  TEST
title: Reading four times high on the reactor
context: Iteration 4 is the final photometer build, with the component positions fixed, TPU-lined mounts so the glass is not scratched, and snap-in covers along the light path to block room light. This is the first time it went onto the reactor and got read against a benchtop instrument on the same culture.

body.v: Fitted it in line on the TFF loop and took a reading against the benchtop BioDrop.
The BioDrop needs 2 mL per reading, which is a lot to take out of a running loop.
Got a first reading roughly four times high.
That is an offset, not drift. A loose rail drifts, so we knew it was not the rail.
Used Developer Mode to see both raw channels and rule them out.
It holds the LED on and streams the raw sample and reference values. Both read cleanly, which left the blank as the only term they share.
It was written to debug this and stayed as a permanent feature.
Found the flow cuvette cannot be cleaned while it is inline, so the blank was taken through a dirty window.
Joshua suggested typing the blank in by hand instead of measuring it. Chars patched that the same evening.
The target agreed beforehand was 10 percent. We are 33 percent low, and the correction overshoots the other way.
This is the second blanking failure on this instrument. Iteration 2 blanked on medium, this one blanked through a dirty cuvette.
Rows 3 and 4 are blank because the repeats were never run. The before-patch value was never written down, only the ratio.

photos: photometer inline on the TFF loop
decision: Did not pass, but we know why
A 4× error is an offset, not drift. A loose rail drifts, so it wasn’t the rail.
The correction overshoots. We now read under the BioDrop, not over it.
counter: One paired reading. Three repeats and a dilution series before this number goes on the wiki.
serial output after the patch
cuvette in the return leg

problems.what: In-line cuvette cannot be cleaned before blanking, and the whole result rests on one pair
problems.fix: Add a flush line, then repeat on three separate cultures before we quote the number.

next: Start the long run and see whether it holds calibration on its own.

subtitle: PHOTOMETER · LONG RUN  ·  TEST
title: Starting the nineteen-day run
context: We had checked the photometer against a benchtop reading once, with someone watching. What we did not know was whether it holds up over days on its own. The reactor was running anyway, so we logged the whole thing from 21 July.

body.v: Logged sample and reference illuminance, the ratio, a rejection rate, the point count and elapsed time.
Roughly one reading every nine minutes.
Served it on a live dashboard over the local network.
Local network only, so nobody can check it from home. There is no alert of any kind, it only draws.
Reached 291 points at one day in, with a sample to reference ratio of 7.33.
The optics were designed for 10 to 1. We noted the gap and did not explain it.
Bubble rejection read zero percent, which we did not question at the time. On other runs it has hit 43 percent.
Left it running rather than tearing it down to chase the ratio.
The ratio is a calibration problem we can come back to. The only way to find out whether it survives nineteen days unattended is to leave it alone.
TABLE 21
Dashboard reading confirmed independently against the Discord record. Both give 291 points and 7.33×.

decision: Let it run rather than stop to fix the ratio
The ratio being off is a calibration question. Whether it survives nineteen days alone is a different one, and the only way to answer it is to leave it running.
counter: Tearing it down to chase the 7.33× straight away. We picked the endurance question over the accuracy one and that’s a real trade.

problems.what: Sample to reference sits at 7.33× against a designed 10:1
problems.fix: Measure both channels with the cuvette empty, then blanked, and compare.

problems.what: No pass condition set, and no written bubble rejection rule
problems.fix: Decide what counts as holding calibration, and dig the rejection rule out of the firmware.

next: Keep it running. Watch the shape of the curve, not just where it ends up.

subtitle: PHOTOMETER · PUMP FAILURE  ·  FAILURE DIAGNOSIS
title: The photometer catches the pump failing
context: The run had been going since 21 July and the curve was not the shape any of us expected. We spent most of the week arguing about why, then on 1 August it dropped and stayed down.

body.v: A healthy culture does not do that. We still cannot explain the shape.
Guessed contamination when it dropped, that we were watching a second organism take over.
That was wrong. We have left it in the record.
Found the recirculation pump had failed. Chars confirmed on inspection and replaced it the same evening.
Nobody was rostered to check the trace daily, which is why the drop was noticed late.
Did not run the flush and reblank that would have separated fouling from biology.
Once the run was torn down the chance was gone.
Our first hypothesis was contamination. It was the pump. Chars confirmed on inspection and replaced it the same evening.

photos: Nineteen days of continuous logging. No exponential phase at any point, a growth rate that fell away steadily, no plateau, then a rebound part way through. On 1 August the trace dropped sharply and stayed down.
decision: Replace the pump and leave the trace intact
The photometer caught a failure in the reactor with nobody watching, which is what we built it to be able to do.
counter: The flush-and-reblank test that would have separated fouling from biology. Once the run is torn down you can’t go back, and we didn’t do it.
trace recovering
loop back in service

problems.what: SINCE W21
problems.fix: Run plate counts alongside OD next time and check whether OD tracks biomass at all.

problems.what: Flush and reblank never run
problems.fix: Do it at the start of the next run, before anything fouls.

next: Plot this trace with the pump-death event annotated. It is the hardware page’s headline figure.

subtitle: BIOREACTOR · PINCH VALVE  ·  DECISION
title: Decision matrix [Pinch valve actuator]
context: Prof. Chang told us in June we had no way to push protectant out of the membrane, so we built a stepper pinch valve. This week we replaced it, on criteria written before we scored anything.

body.v: Wrote the criteria first so they could not be bent toward the answer we wanted.
Whether it holds when power is cut. Holding force against the permeate pressure. Whether we can build it from parts already in the lab. How much firmware it needs.
Scored a stepper, a servo and a solenoid out of five on each.
The solenoid is unscored rather than zero. We could not source one in time.
Chose the servo on the first criterion alone.
A stepper lets go when it loses power and the loop is full of live culture. A servo stays tight. Holding on power loss is a safety property, so it outranks the other three.
The servo we used is a spare from the VEX kit, not a part chosen for this.
The inlet hole needs to be 4 mm and the outlet 6 mm, with tolerance added at CAD.
Neither of us has measured what pressure the valve actually needs to hold against.
TABLE 23
Scored out of 5 by each of us, then averaged. Row 3 is unscored, not zero. We could not source one in time.

decision: Servo pinch valve
A stepper lets go when it loses power and the loop is full of live culture, so holding on power loss outranks the other criteria.
counter: The stepper we’d already built and knew worked. The effort already spent on it is not a reason to keep it.

problems.what: Scores are ours, not measured
problems.fix: Bench-test the holding force and power draw, then rescore rows 2 and 4.

next: Print the servo version with tolerance added and check the fit before committing the CAD.

subtitle: BIOREACTOR · ASSEMBLY  ·  BUILD
title: Assembling the full rig
context: The valve, the sensors and the photometer had all been built separately. This is the week the whole thing went together as one machine.

body.v: Mounted the hollow fibre module first, lumen ports facing up.
Air clears on fill rather than sitting in the fibres. The ports are not marked on the module, so the orientation has to be remembered.
cross-flow loop plumbed
electronics wired
Plumbed the cross-flow loop and wired the electronics.
Fitted the pressure transducer and put the photometer into the return leg.
Downstream of the pump rather than before it, which is a longer plumb. The pump puts a pulse into the flow, and putting the beam after it gives that pulse some line length to smooth out in.
Photographed the build across four days without agreeing what to photograph.
Nineteen images with gaps, duplicates and no captions. We cannot work out the assembly order from them.
TABLE 23a
Table 23a. Parts as fitted, not as drawn. The photometer sits downstream of the pump so pulsation is damped before the beam.

decision: Photometer downstream of the pump
The pump puts a sawtooth into the flow. We saw it in the pressure trace on 12 July.
Putting the beam after the pump means the pulse has some line length to smooth out in.
counter: Upstream, which is shorter and easier to plumb. It would have put the pulsation straight into the optical reading.

problems.what: Nineteen build photographs uncaptioned
problems.fix: Caption each one with date, what it shows, and which assembly step it belongs to.

problems.what: No written assembly order for the rig
problems.fix: Write it now from the photos, while the order is still in someone’s head.

problems.what: SINCE W18
problems.fix: Mark them, so the next person fitting it does not have to guess the orientation.

next: Print the servo valve and fit it after the membrane.

subtitle: BIOREACTOR · NEXT PHASE  ·  WEEK
title: Where the bioreactor stands on 13 August
context: This is the last week the notebook covers, not the last week of work. The bioreactor is part way through a rebuild and three problems are open, all of them mechanical. We had expected the biology to be the hard part.

body.v: Started moving from the peristaltic pump to a magnetic one.
A magnetic pump can be driven from the Arduino, which is what lets the system run without someone standing over it.
It is weaker and cannot lift liquid out of the serum bottle.
Planned a PC-cooler-style clear rectangle with ports top and bottom to get round the head problem.
Feed in at the top, draw from the bottom, so gravity does some of the work. It was bought for its shape, not because it is designed for this.
Found the dissolved oxygen and pH probes do not fit the reservoir cap.
The cap has to be bored out. Keeping it airtight is the harder part, because the sensor body is thicker than its cable and the plug thicker again.
Designed a cap in two halves that clamps around the cable and screws shut.
Airtight, and nothing gets cut. The first approach was cutting each cable, threading it, and soldering it back.
Sketched a sealed cartridge for replenishing B. subtilis, on the printer ink model.
It opens only once it is inside the box, so a farmer can top up without a biosafety problem.
That creates a second problem. Dead cells clog the loop and block the photometer, so it needs a flush into a waste box.
Wetted and tested the new membrane on 15 August, just past the end of this notebook.
BIOREACTOR
No second containment stage, now that the 0.2 µm claim is narrower than we thought
Foaming from B. subtilis surfactant. Raised twice by Prof. Chang, no design response
Prototype II changed three variables at once, so stirring is not proven on its own
DO and pH probes do not fit the reservoir cap, and the vessel has to stay airtight
No way to clear dead cells from the loop before they block the photometer
Nineteen build photographs from 3–7 August are uncaptioned
PHOTOMETER
No dilution series, so the response is not known to be linear. Doubling gave 1.56×, not 2×
Reference channel moved between readings minutes apart. A reference should not do that
Bubble rejection has read 0 % and 43 % on different runs. The rule is not written down
Sample to reference sits at 5–7× against optics designed for 10×
One paired reading against the BioDrop. No repeats
Missing exponential phase and no plateau across the whole nineteen-day run
Flush and reblank never run, so fouling was never separated from biology
LIGHT PLATE
The lux to PPFD conversion factor we used is not written down anywhere
Well-to-well output never measured. It is the acceptance criterion from 19 May
TEMP_BASE 32 °C and TEMP_MAX 50 °C are plausible guesses, not measurements
Has never driven a real CcaS–CcaR experiment
PLANT SIDE
Imaging station lighting evenness across the plate never measured
Floating plate buoyancy never verified with a full set of plants on it
Humidity box has no recorded target range and no logged performance

decision: Design around the weak pump rather than revert
Arduino control is the difference between automated and somebody standing there. The peristaltic pump can’t give us that.
counter: Going back to the peristaltic pump. It works, and it would cost us the automation this design depends on.

problems.what: DO and pH probes do not fit the cap
problems.fix: Bore the cap out, then print the two-half clamp cap for the cables.

problems.what: No way to clear dead cells from the loop
problems.fix: Design the flush and the waste box at the same time as the cartridge.

next: Modify the PC cooler cap so the sensors fit. Design the printed cap that clamps round the wire.
